title: A term paper, written instead of an exam, gave us Huffman coding
body: In 1951, MIT professor Robert Fano gave his information theory students a choice: sit the final exam or write a term paper on finding the most efficient binary code. David Huffman was about to give up when he hit on building the code from the bottom up: count each symbol, then keep tying the two rarest together into one branch until a single tree remains. Common symbols end up with short codes and rare ones with long codes, and no method that encodes symbols one at a time does better. Prefix codes like his, often called Huffman codes, still help compress ZIP files, JPEGs and MP3s.

slides.question: A fixed 3-bit code stores ABRACADABRA in 33 bits. How many bits will Huffman's code need?
slides.explanation: 23 bits. A appears 5 times and gets a 1-bit code; B, R, C and D, 6 letters in all, get 3 bits each: 5 + 18 = 23.

slides.alt: Animation on a cork board: index cards for the letters of ABRACADABRA, counted 5, 2, 2, 1 and 1, are tied together with red string two rarest at a time into a tree. Left strings read 0 and right ones 1, giving A the code 0 and the word 23 bits instead of 33.

slides.prompt: Tap ‘Tie the two rarest’ until one tree is left. Then type your own word and build its code.
slides.takeaway: Common letters sit near the top with short codes, rare ones deep down with long codes, and no code starts another, so the bits need no separators.

slides.heading: Bits to store ABRACADABRA
slides.note: 11 letters; plain text often spends 8 bits on each.

slides.heading: No gaps needed
slides.text: In a Huffman code, no letter's code is the start of another's. So a decoder reading 0110111… always knows where each letter ends: 0 is A, 110 is B, 111 is R. Nothing has to separate them.

slides.heading: The student beat the teacher
slides.text: Fano had worked with Claude Shannon on a similar code, built from the top down. Huffman's bottom-up tree is guaranteed to give the shortest code of its kind; their Shannon–Fano coding isn't.

slides.question: Two cards tie for rarest, and you could tie either pair first. What happens?
options: Either way works just as well
Only one choice gives the best code
You must start again from the top
slides.explanation: A Huffman code need not be unique: different choices can give different codes, but each is a Huffman code and none uses more bits in total.
